display.text: The parameter μ₁ − μ₂ comparing two groups' average responses. A negative value means population 1 has a lower mean; reversing group order reverses the sign.
The statistic ȳ₁ − ȳ₂, used to estimate μ₁ − μ₂ from two groups' observed responses.
A test comparing population means of a quantitative response in two independent groups, usually testing H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Also called two-sample t-test.

For small independent samples, the quantitative response should be reasonably normal within each population; strong skewness or outliers can undermine the t approximation. Larger samples can support approximate inference.
The estimated sampling spread of the difference between independent sample means. In Welch's procedure it is √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

response.correctResponse: standard error of the difference in means

display.text: An interval estimating μ₁ − μ₂ and showing the direction, size, and precision of a mean difference. Exclusion of zero corresponds to rejection by a matching two-sided t test at the corresponding significance level.
The observed difference between sample means minus the hypothesized difference, divided by its standard error. For the usual null, the hypothesized difference is zero.
An independent-samples t-test that does not assume equal population variances. It uses SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) and an approximate t distribution with adjusted degrees of freedom.
